deep.reconstruction:
This page sets up the physical hypothesis of E260. Euler wants a quantitative law for the observed loss of motion of water in pipes. On the previous page he attributed that loss to friction of the water against the tube walls.

§5: The smallest fluid particles can be treated as small solids. Where they slide along and 'graze' the walls, they must undergo friction. That friction obeys the same laws as solid friction, though it is much smaller in magnitude because of the particles' great 'lubricity'.

§6: He recalls the Amontons law of solid friction. Friction is a fixed fraction of the normal force pressing the body onto the surface, and is independent of the body's shape and of the area of contact. For wood or metal on wood or metal, without notable roughness, experiments give a coefficient of about 1/4 or sometimes 1/3.

§7: By analogy, he postulates for every portion of fluid a frictional force F = λ·N. Here N is the force with which that portion is pressed against the tube wall, i.e. the hydrostatic or hydrodynamic pressure times the wetted area. λ is to be found by experiment and may depend on the pipe material, so it is kept as an indefinite parameter in the calculation.

§8 begins the model for water flowing through the tube ABCD (Tab. VI, Fig. 1). The next page completes it. Wall pressure on the element is ρ g p u ds, where p is the pressure head, u the wetted perimeter and ds the element length. Friction is λ p u ds. The element's mass is z² ds, where z² is the cross-sectional area. So the deceleration is λ p u / z², which is a hydraulic-radius (perimeter/area) law.

In modern terms this is a Coulomb-type wall-friction closure for one-dimensional pipe hydraulics. Friction is proportional to pressure rather than to a power of velocity, and it feeds into Euler's one-dimensional unsteady pipe-flow equations.
errors: The physical hypothesis is wrong for fluids. Wall shear in pipe flow is essentially independent of the static pressure level and depends on velocity: linearly in laminar flow, roughly quadratically in turbulent flow. A pressure-proportional friction would make losses depend on the absolute pressure, contrary to experiment.

§4 (previous page) claims that nobody had investigated the laws of fluid friction. This overlooks Newton, Principia Book II, Section IX, which hypothesizes that resistance from 'defectus lubricitatis' is proportional to relative velocity.

Next page (not this one): for a circular section of diameter n, the perimeter is πn and the area πn²/4, so u/z² = 4/n, the same as the square. Euler's 'u = 2πn, zz = πnn' corresponds to a radius n, so 2λp/n holds only if n is the radius.

ideas.what: Fluid particles treated as small solids subject to Amontons/Coulomb friction against the walls
ideas.modern_name: Coulomb (dry-friction) wall-shear closure; pressure-dependent wall friction
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler, E260 (an abandoned hypothesis); the friction law itself to Amontons 1699 and Coulomb 1781
ideas.where_published: E260 itself; discussed by Truesdell in the Opera Omnia II.12/II.13 introductions (unsure of exact location)

ideas.what: Solid friction proportional to the normal load, independent of contact area and shape, with coefficient about 1/4 to 1/3
ideas.where_published: Euler, 'Sur le frottement des corps solides' (E62, 1748)

ideas.what: Friction coefficient kept as an undetermined parameter to be fitted to pipe experiments, possibly depending on the pipe material
ideas.modern_name: Empirical friction factor (precursor of Darcy–Weisbach/Chézy coefficients)

deep.surprise_reason: The page states a well-known (and physically mistaken) Coulomb-friction hypothesis for pipe flow. This hypothesis is already recorded in histories of hydraulics and in Truesdell's commentary; there is nothing unrecorded here.
